items.title: 5.4.1 Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces (London dispersion forces)

source_refs.note: Topic 5.4.1, printed pages 98-100, as printed: Tables 5.1 and 5.2, Figure 5.2 (original drawing) and Quick Check 5.2. The print's 'Isodecane (C20H42)' is marked as a book error.

blocks.title: Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole force
blocks.text: The momentary force of attraction between an instantaneous dipole and an induced dipole is called instantaneous dipole-induced dipole force.
These are only forces that exist among the molecules of non-polar compounds. The strength of these forces depend upon the following factors

When the molecular mass (Mᵣ) of a compound is greater, the id-id forces are stronger and vice versa. This is because in a larger atom or molecule the dispersion of electronic cloud and polarisation is relatively easier. This factor operates in the halogen and noble gas families. The physical state changes in the halogen family from top to bottom due to the increase in size and polarizability. The first two members in the halogen family (F₂ and Cl₂) are gases, but bromine is a liquid and iodine a solid (b.p. = 458 K). The boiling points of noble gases in group 18 also increase from helium (He) to xenon (Xe) as in Table 5.1.

blocks.caption: Table 5.1 Molar masses and boiling points of group 17 and 18 of periodic table.

blocks.text: A molecule with larger surface area has more number of contacts for a nearby molecule. Thus the forces among the molecules of a compound having larger surface area are stronger. Consider saturated hydrocarbons. These have chains of carbon atoms linked with hydrogen atoms. Compare the length of the chains in C₂H₆ and C₆H₁₄. They have the boiling points −88.6 °C and 68.7 °C, respectively. It is evident that the molecules with larger chain length experiences stronger attractive forces. The reason is that longer molecules have more places along the length where they can be attracted to other molecules. Boiling points of some hydrocarbons are given in Table 5.2.

blocks.caption: Table 5.2 Boiling points and physical states of some hydrocarbons

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Table 5.2 prints “Isodecane (C₂₀H₄₂)”. C₂₀H₄₂ is icosane (eicosane), the straight-chain alkane with 20 carbon atoms, boiling point about 343 °C and solid at room temperature; isodecane is a branched isomer of decane, C₁₀H₂₂.

Three isomers of pentane have the same relative molecular mass (Mᵣ), however, they differ in their surface areas. Straight chain pentane has largest surface area and so is its boiling point among the three isomers of pentane. 2-Methylbutane (Isopentane) has smaller surface area than n-pentane but larger than 2,2-Dimethylpropane (Neopentane). Therefore, the forces among 2-Methylbutane molecules are intermediate and the least strong forces occur in 2,2-Dimethylpropane. The isomers of pentane alone with their boiling points are given in Figure 5.2.

blocks.alt: Three condensed structural formulas on pink shapes outlining each molecule. Pentane (n-pentane): H3C-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3 as a zigzag chain, b.p. 36.2 degrees C. 2-Methylbutane (iso-pentane): a chain H3C-CH-CH2-CH3 with a CH3 branch on the second carbon, b.p. 28 degrees C. 2,2-Dimethylpropane (neo-pentane): a central carbon joined to four CH3 groups, compact shape, b.p. 9.5 degrees C.
